source.title: On Privileged and Convergent Bases in Neural Network Representations
source.authors: Davis Brown; Nikhil Vyas; Yamini Bansal

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies whether neural representations have privileged or convergent neuron bases, not whether individual neurons respond to semantically unrelated inputs. Its results address an adjacent interpretability question but do not test any listed version of polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The paper does not identify neurons by their input semantics or measure mixed responses, so it does not test whether neurons have one coherent job. Rows below record adjacent results about representational bases; they are linked to none of the claim versions. Cited examples and results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper measures neuron-basis alignment across runs (perm-corr), LMC barriers, and whether retraining can undo random rotations. It never examines what inputs individual neurons respond to, so it does not measure polysemanticity or its causes. It bears on whether the neuron basis is privileged, which is adjacent to the claim. That finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors add three points. Rotation non-invariance shows the neuron basis is significant. LMC overstates cross-run neuron similarity, with LMC gains driven partly by noise robustness. Appendix A finds a linear residual stream does not explain the convergence from frozen early layers.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies basis alignment, rotation recovery, and linear mode connectivity; it does not apply the original neuron-interpretation or polysemanticity measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that basis correlation changes when early layers are frozen identically; rotation-related error worsens for later layers. It also reports width-dependent changes in LMC barriers, but nearly constant perm-corr.

fits_no_version.finding: Retraining later layers cannot undo random orthonormal rotations of pre-activations in a Myrtle-CNN. The resulting error is similar to using random features, so the neuron basis matters (privileged basis).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In nonlinear vision CNNs the neuron basis is privileged: arbitrary rotations of layer representations are not recoverable by retraining later layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Perm-corr between independently initialized ResNet20s stays nearly constant from 1x to 32x width. It is lower for trained pairs than for random pairs at most widths. Freezing two early blocks raises it in ConvNeXt and ViT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently trained networks do not converge to a shared neuron basis, but sharing frozen early layers induces convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: The LMC barrier without permutation shrinks with width, and so does the accuracy drop from averaging with a random network. The authors attribute LMC gains to noise robustness rather than basis similarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains in linear mode connectivity with width overstate neuron-level similarity across runs.

record.problems: The paper does not measure semantic responses of individual neurons. Several relevant trends are described qualitatively while plotted values appear only in figures; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Other adjacent basis-alignment, identity-stitching, and width-sweep plots in Sections 3 and 5 and Appendix A were not separately extracted because they do not measure polysemanticity; the retained rows capture the main reported trends relevant to the neighboring basis question.

untested.parts: All: no analysis of what inputs image-classifier neurons respond to.
All: no language-model MLP neurons studied.
All: superposition and feature counts are not measured.
All: initialization varies across runs, but the polysemanticity of the resulting neurons is not measured.
All: residual-stream structure and width are varied, but only basis alignment is measured, not the share of polysemantic neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is related only through the 'privileged basis' premise that makes neuron-level interpretation, and thus polysemanticity, meaningful. It contains no measurement of mixed neuron responses. The appendix rows (modified ResNet-20, width effects) were left out appropriately as adjacent results.

versions.untested_parts: Whether image-classifier neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, including the stated InceptionV1 example.
Whether MLP neurons in language models respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how prevalence varies by layer.
Whether superposition causes polysemanticity through capacity pressure.
Whether initialization, regularization, or training noise produce polysemantic neurons without capacity pressure.
Whether architecture, activation function, or regularization changes the share of polysemantic neurons or lowers it without substantial performance loss.
Whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a feature or whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare.
Whether polysemanticity classifications depend on activation range or explanation-scoring method.

rows.subject: Resnet20 (widest model Resnet20-32x)
rows.operation_detail: Measured permutation-correlation between networks trained with independent initializations and batch orderings across width.
rows.note: The text describes the trend; the figure contains the plotted values. This measures basis alignment, not semantic polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Resnet20 (widest model Resnet20-32x)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the linear mode connectivity barrier without permuting neurons.
rows.value: The barrier improves significantly with width.
rows.note: The authors interpret the improvement as not necessarily indicating increased basis similarity.

rows.subject: Resnet20 (widths not individually stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared permutation-correlation for pairs of trained networks with pairs of random networks.
rows.value: Two random networks have higher perm-corr than two trained networks at all but the narrowest width.
rows.note: The text states the comparison; exact plotted values are not reported in prose.

rows.subject: Myrtle-CNN
rows.stage_stated: trained to 92% accuracy, then retrained after rotation
rows.operation_detail: Rotated and froze successive early-layer pre-activations, then retrained the remaining layers.
rows.baseline: Trained network accuracy 92%; baseline error not stated
rows.value: Figure only; text says error degrades significantly and worsens for later layers.
rows.note: The comparison is with random-feature performance; this tests whether rotated representations can be recovered, not whether neurons have mixed semantic responses.
rows.check: Text cites 'Figure 4' for rotation results but the plot is Figure 2. The comparator is the random-feature error, not the 92% baseline. The 'numbers_found 1/1' refers only to the 92% selection accuracy, not a result value.
